html:
It has been bitterly cold in K County these past two days. Yesterday the low was −31 °C. Today is a little milder, but it actually feels colder. Mom and Dad said it several times today: “How can it be this cold?!”

I slept badly on my second night after landing in H City, and again last night. I was exhausted, but once I lay down I couldn’t fall asleep. Scenes kept running through my head like a film, some replayed, some imagined, of what it would be like once I got home; my relatives’ words and faces circled in my mind, around and around.

Every time I see my parents, it seems we need a little while to get used to each other again. There is always a bit of stiffness at first. It was like that the last two times too, when we met up somewhere else for a trip. Yesterday at noon they picked me up, we had lunch with relatives and went home, and even at dinner it was still a little awkward.

Today is Mom’s sixtieth birthday, the main reason I came back this time. The plan had been to go to B City for shopping, new clothes and a meal, but they both said no, we’ll do all that here in K. K County doesn’t have many clothing stores, and only a handful are good enough for Mom. Those count as the top shops in town.

The top end of K County retail is monopolized by “Yansha.” After a top and a pair of pants, we went to another Yansha store. Mom tried on two pieces, each around 700 or 800 yuan, and afterwards didn’t say much: the reaction of someone who likes what she sees. She put them down, walked out of the shop, and said another place had something similar, cheaper. Just as I suspected: she had put them down because they were too expensive. So I dragged the two of them back in and bought both. At yet another shop we bought a padded winter jacket, and then, at their urgent insistence, the shopping spree came to an end.

In the years since she retired, Mom has gradually started caring about her appearance: skincare, shopping, clothes. Clothes above all are her great weakness. In 2019 she sold off her little stall and formally ended a working life of more than thirty years. In her early years she was a tailor, cutting and sewing, right up until my final year of high school, the year of the gaokao, China’s college entrance exam, when she stayed home for a year to look after me. Once I went off to university she started a little lingerie stall, and kept that going for another twelve years. Of the 365 days in a year she worked at least 360, staying home only a couple of days at New Year, and even then she’d grumble that every day she didn’t go in was a day’s money lost. That kind of work has two drawbacks: lunch, and the winter cold. Now and then we brought her food, but mostly she bought something, and since she wouldn’t spend money on herself, she usually just made do. An occasional treat meant malatang, a spicy soup of skewered vegetables and meat. Whether at the tailoring shop or the lingerie stall, the winters were brutally cold. Back then her greatest wish was simply to have a warm room to sit in through the winter. Thinking about it now, I don’t really understand why the places where people ran these businesses were so grim. Why not turn the heating up a bit, even if it cost a little more? Maybe the small traders didn’t want to spend the money, and the mall didn’t want to push up the rent and make the stalls harder to let.

With less than an hour to go before lunch, we decided to go home first. That’s the beauty of a small county town, and our place is near the center, so everything is easy to get to, nearly always within a ten-minute walk. Mom began trying on her new clothes one by one, then gave me a tour of her wardrobe, and laughed: “Look at your mom, what a show-off!” Being a seamstress herself, and very particular about clothes, she often alters what she buys, or else takes it back. Dad chimed in from the side: “Your mom’s clothes? She returns a ton every year!” I had bought her three blouses; she tried them on over and over, finally settled on one, and then decided which pants and which shoes to wear with it.

At half past eleven we got to the restaurant next to our building, which is also the fanciest restaurant in K County. The three of us deliberated for ages and chose four dishes: wooden-bucket tofu, cold beef tripe salad, fish poached in fiery chili broth, and (I forget the fourth…). The cake we’d ordered before going shopping arrived with exactly six candles. The restaurant gave us a bowl of longevity noodles, the traditional birthday dish, and a fruit platter on the house, and the birthday banquet was officially underway! We talked happily, and they drank happily: six bottles of beer between the two of them. That familiar feeling of home was back. The awkward first day was safely behind us.

Once Mom had hit her drinking stride, she went out to the restroom. Dad immediately turned to me: “Go and see your Third Aunt”—his sister; Chinese families number aunts and uncles by birth order. “When I brought it up on our video call the other day, you didn’t say a word.” I hesitated for two seconds, then said, “Mm.” Dad said it would really be for his sake. I said, “If you put it that way, then I’ll go.” “She’s not a good person… but what can you do? She’s my own sister.” More than ten years ago I fell ill and was in hospital, and we needed money. Things were tight at home and Dad wasn’t well, so Mom and I didn’t dare tell him; instead we went to Third Aunt to borrow money. She refused, and Mom had a huge row with her. Several other unpleasant episodes followed, and for all these years relations between the two families have blown hot and cold. I have never felt close to her. Growing up I didn’t see much of her; only as a kid, when we visited my eldest aunt on Mom’s side, I’d often go over to play with Third Aunt’s daughters, my cousins. As an adult I’ve seen even less of her.

We were home before three, and between fiddling with our phones and watching TV, it was soon dinnertime. Stir-fried chicken with broccoli, flash-fried cabbage, sticky bean buns, millet porridge: dinner, done. Then the two of them went back to their phones and the TV, and I put on my headphones and read some of Walter Isaacson’s biography of Elon Musk. Then my cousin video-called to wish Mom a happy birthday. She divorced more than ten years ago and has been drifting from place to place ever since; now she does housekeeping work in Beijing. She gets her jobs through JD.com’s platform, so I suppose she counts as an employee of a tech giant. It was past eight in the evening when she called; she had just finished her last job of the day and was having dinner. She is cheerful and optimistic by nature; I tease her that she hasn’t a care in the world. However hard life gets, she can always laugh out loud. Her daughter dropped out after a few days of middle school and has done odd jobs here and there. After my cousin’s father died a while ago, my niece went back to Beijing and hasn’t found work since. In 2023 the economy was bad all over the world, and people like them, the so-called “low-end population,” as Beijing officials once labeled migrant workers, were hit hard. My niece is only 27 this year, her future is hazy, and whenever the family mentions her, they sigh.

The call ended after nine. My parents went to bed, and I went to my room and lay down, read more of the Musk biography, video-chatted with my wife for a while, and that was day two at home. The end.
